title: Handling Missing Data IV - KNN Imputer
abstract:
The first multivariate imputer. Where mean and median imputation look only
at the column being filled, the KNN Imputer uses the other rows and the other
columns: it finds the $k$ most similar complete rows and fills the gap with their
values. This document covers the algorithm, the nan_euclidean distance
that makes it work when the neighbours are themselves incomplete, the
uniform-versus-distance weighting, why feature scaling is mandatory here, the
choice of $k$, and the accuracy-versus-cost tradeoff the notes flag.

blocks.t: The Idea
From the notes
KNN Imputer (Multivariate Imputation)

items: Other rows are also used to impute the values.

Works on the KNN algorithm — characteristics similar to
 neighbours.
Replace the value with the nearest neighbours.
More accurate but more time taking.

blocks.t: The shift from univariate to multivariate

Median imputation answers "what is a typical weight?" KNN imputation answers
"what is a typical weight for someone like this person?" The second is a
strictly better question whenever the columns are related — and if they are not
related, you should not be using a multivariate method at all.

blocks.cap:
Age and weight are correlated. Median imputation places every imputed
 point on a single horizontal line, destroying the relationship. KNN imputation
 places each point near the trend, because it looks at the age of the row it is
 filling.

blocks.t: The Algorithm

items: Take a row with a missing value in column $j$.

Compute its distance to every other row, using only the columns that both
 rows have present.
Take the $k$ nearest rows that do have a value in column $j$.

Fill the gap with the mean of those $k$ values (or a distance-weighted
 mean).

blocks.t: The distance problem, and nan_euclidean

Ordinary Euclidean distance is undefined when either row has a missing value —
which is precisely the situation we are in.

blocks.cap:
The fix: compute the distance over the columns present in both rows,
 then rescale as if all columns had been present.

blocks.t: The nan_euclidean metric

For rows $x$ and $y$ with $p$ total columns, let $P$ be the set of columns
present in both:

The factor $p/|P|$ is the essential part. Without it, a pair of rows sharing only
two columns would appear closer than a pair sharing all ten, simply
because fewer squared terms were summed — and the imputer would
systematically prefer the least informative neighbours. The rescaling makes
distances comparable across different overlap patterns.

If $|P| = 0$ — the two rows share no observed column — the distance is
undefined and scikit-learn falls back to the column mean.
Weighting

rows: All $k$ neighbours contribute equally: $\hat x_j = \frac1k\sum_{i\in N_k} x_{ij}$
Nearer neighbours count more: $\hat x_j = \dfrac{\sum_i w_i x_{ij}}{\sum_i w_i}$ with $w_i = 1/d_i$

blocks.t:
Distance weighting is usually slightly better, and it degrades more gracefully
when $k$ is set too large — a distant neighbour contributes little rather than
a full $1/k$ share.
Scaling Is Mandatory
The mistake that silently ruins KNN imputation

KNN imputation is built on distances, and distances are dominated by whichever
column has the largest numeric range (Topic 13). If salary is in tens of
thousands and age is in tens, the "nearest neighbours" are simply the
rows with the most similar salary — age contributes nothing to the distance,
and the imputation is effectively univariate on salary.

Scale before imputing. But this creates a chicken-and-egg problem:
StandardScaler needs complete data to compute a mean. The resolution is
that scikit-learn's scalers ignore NaN when computing statistics, so
StandardScaler $\to$ KNNImputer works correctly in a pipeline. If
you need the values back on their original scale, apply
scaler.inverse_transform afterwards.
Choosing $k$, and the Cost

blocks.cap:
Left: the notes' "more time taking" claim, measured. KNN imputation
 is $O(n^2p)$ against $O(np)$ for a simple imputer, and the gap widens with $n$.
 Right: $k$ is a hyperparameter — small $k$ is noisy, and large $k$ converges
 to the column mean, discarding the whole benefit.

blocks.t: Why it is expensive

Filling one missing cell requires the distance from its row to every other row:
$O(np)$. With $m$ missing cells the total is $O(mnp)$, and in the worst case
$m=O(n)$ giving $O(n^2p)$. There is no training phase to amortise this against
— exactly the instance-based cost profile of Topic 04, since the imputer
is a KNN model.

Consequences: it becomes impractical past roughly $10^5$ rows, and it must store
the entire training matrix for use at serving time — so your model artefact is
no longer a few kilobytes.

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: More accurate — uses the relationships between columns
More time taking — $O(n^2p)$, no training phase to amortise
Preserves correlations that univariate methods destroy
Requires the full training matrix at serving time
Requires feature scaling, or it silently degrades
Degrades in high dimensions (curse of dimensionality, Topic 32)
Naturally handles ordinal and binary columns

blocks.t: When it is not worth it

If the columns are close to independent, the nearest neighbours carry no extra
information about the missing column and KNN imputation reduces to an expensive
mean. Check the correlation matrix first: if the column you are filling
correlates weakly with everything else, use the median and spend your effort
elsewhere.
Code

import numpy as np, pandas as pd, time
from sklearn.impute import KNNImputer, SimpleImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.metrics import pairwise_distances
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, GridSearchCV, train_test_split

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 2000
age    = rng.uniform(20, 70, n)
weight = 0.9 * age + 30 + rng.normal(0, 4, n)        # correlated with age
salary = 2500 * age + rng.normal(0, 20_000, n)       # also correlated
X_true = np.c_[age, weight, salary]

mask = rng.random(n) < .25
X = X_true.copy(); X[mask, 1] = np.nan                # weight is missing

# =====================================================================
# 1. UNIVARIATE vs MULTIVARIATE -- measured on the values we hid
# =====================================================================
med = SimpleImputer(strategy="median").fit_transform(X)
knn = KNNImputer(n_neighbors=5).fit_transform(X)

mae = lambda v: np.abs(v[mask, 1] - X_true[mask, 1]).mean()
print(f"median imputation MAE {mae(med):.3f}")
print(f"KNN    imputation MAE {mae(knn):.3f}")

# the relationship, preserved or destroyed:
print("true correlation age~weight     :", np.corrcoef(X_true[:,0], X_true[:,1])[0,1].round(3))
print("after median imputation         :", np.corrcoef(med[:,0], med[:,1])[0,1].round(3))
print("after KNN imputation            :", np.corrcoef(knn[:,0], knn[:,1])[0,1].round(3))

# =====================================================================
# 2. THE nan_euclidean DISTANCE, FROM SCRATCH
# =====================================================================
def nan_euclidean(x, y):
    """Distance over shared columns, rescaled to the full dimension."""
    present = ~np.isnan(x) & ~np.isnan(y)
    if present.sum() == 0:
        return np.nan
    p, k = len(x), present.sum()
    return np.sqrt(p / k * ((x[present] - y[present]) ** 2).sum())

a = np.array([3.0, np.nan, 7.0, 2.0])
b = np.array([3.2, 5.0,    6.8, 2.1])
c = np.array([3.1, 4.9,    np.nan, 2.4])
print(f"\nd(a,b) = {nan_euclidean(a,b):.4f}  (3 shared columns)")
print(f"d(a,c) = {nan_euclidean(a,c):.4f}  (2 shared columns)")
print("sklearn agrees:",
      pairwise_distances(a.reshape(1,-1), b.reshape(1,-1),
                         metric="nan_euclidean")[0,0].round(4))

# WITHOUT the p/k rescaling, fewer shared columns would look CLOSER:
raw = lambda x,y: np.sqrt(np.nansum((x-y)**2 * (~np.isnan(x) & ~np.isnan(y))))
print(f"unscaled: d(a,b)={raw(a,b):.4f}  d(a,c)={raw(a,c):.4f} "
      f"-- c looks closer only because it shares less")

# =====================================================================
# 3. THE ALGORITHM, IMPLEMENTED
# =====================================================================
def knn_impute_column(X, col, k=5):
    X = X.copy()
    missing = np.where(np.isnan(X[:, col]))[0]
    donors  = np.where(~np.isnan(X[:, col]))[0]
    for i in missing:
        d = np.array([nan_euclidean(X[i], X[j]) for j in donors])
        good = ~np.isnan(d)
        nearest = donors[good][np.argsort(d[good])[:k]]
        X[i, col] = X[nearest, col].mean()
    return X

scratch = knn_impute_column(X, col=1, k=5)
print(f"\nscratch MAE {np.abs(scratch[mask,1]-X_true[mask,1]).mean():.3f}"
      f"   sklearn MAE {mae(knn):.3f}")

# =====================================================================
# 4. SCALING IS MANDATORY -- salary otherwise owns the distance
# =====================================================================
unscaled = KNNImputer(n_neighbors=5).fit_transform(X)

scaler = StandardScaler().fit(X)          # sklearn scalers IGNORE NaN
Xs = scaler.transform(X)
scaled = scaler.inverse_transform(KNNImputer(n_neighbors=5).fit_transform(Xs))

print(f"\nunscaled KNN MAE {np.abs(unscaled[mask,1]-X_true[mask,1]).mean():.3f}")
print(f"scaled   KNN MAE {np.abs(scaled[mask,1]-X_true[mask,1]).mean():.3f}")
# Unscaled, "nearest" means "similar salary" and age contributes ~nothing,
# because salary's variance is ~10^8 times age's.
print("variance per column:", np.nanvar(X, axis=0).round(1))

# =====================================================================
# 5. TUNING k AND THE WEIGHTING
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'k':>4s} {'uniform':>9s} {'distance':>9s}")
for k in [1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 25, 50, 200]:
    u = KNNImputer(n_neighbors=k, weights="uniform").fit_transform(Xs)
    d = KNNImputer(n_neighbors=k, weights="distance").fit_transform(Xs)
    fu = scaler.inverse_transform(u); fd = scaler.inverse_transform(d)
    print(f"{k:4d} {np.abs(fu[mask,1]-X_true[mask,1]).mean():9.3f} "
          f"{np.abs(fd[mask,1]-X_true[mask,1]).mean():9.3f}")
# k=1 is noisy; k=200 converges to the column mean, throwing away the benefit.

# =====================================================================
# 6. THE COST -- "more accurate but more time taking"
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'rows':>7s} {'KNNImputer':>12s} {'SimpleImputer':>14s}")
for N in [500, 2000, 8000]:
    A = rng.normal(0, 1, (N, 10)); A[rng.random(A.shape) < .15] = np.nan
    t = time.perf_counter(); KNNImputer(n_neighbors=5).fit_transform(A)
    tk = time.perf_counter() - t
    t = time.perf_counter(); SimpleImputer(strategy="median").fit_transform(A)
    ts = time.perf_counter() - t
    print(f"{N:7d} {tk:11.3f}s {ts:13.4f}s   ({tk/max(ts,1e-9):.0f}x slower)")
# The ratio grows with N -- it is O(n^2 p) against O(n p).

# =====================================================================
# 7. WHEN IT IS NOT WORTH IT -- independent columns
# =====================================================================
Z_true = rng.normal(0, 1, (1500, 5))                  # NO correlation
Z = Z_true.copy(); m2 = rng.random(1500) < .25; Z[m2, 0] = np.nan
e1 = np.abs(SimpleImputer(strategy="median").fit_transform(Z)[m2,0]-Z_true[m2,0]).mean()
e2 = np.abs(KNNImputer(n_neighbors=5).fit_transform(Z)[m2,0]-Z_true[m2,0]).mean()
print(f"\nindependent columns:  median MAE {e1:.3f}   KNN MAE {e2:.3f}")
# Essentially identical. KNN bought you nothing but compute.
# CHECK THE CORRELATION MATRIX BEFORE REACHING FOR IT.

# =====================================================================
# 8. IN A PIPELINE, TUNED, AND FITTED ON TRAIN ONLY
# =====================================================================
y = (0.02 * X_true[:, 1] + 0.00001 * X_true[:, 2] + rng.normal(0, .6, n) > 2.1).astype(int)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.25, random_state=0)

pipe = Pipeline([
    ("scale", StandardScaler()),          # BEFORE the imputer -- mandatory
    ("impute", KNNImputer()),
    ("clf",   LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)),
])
gs = GridSearchCV(pipe, {
    "impute__n_neighbors": [3, 5, 10, 20],
    "impute__weights":     ["uniform", "distance"],
}, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc", n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print("\nbest:", gs.best_params_, round(gs.best_score_, 4))
print("test auc:", round(gs.score(X_te, y_te), 4))

# The fitted imputer stores the TRAINING matrix -- that is what it uses
# to find neighbours for a live request:
print("stored training rows:",
      gs.best_estimator_.named_steps["impute"]._fit_X.shape)
Worked Examples
KNN imputation with $k=2$
Three complete rows and one incomplete row, features $(A, B)$:
(1,2),\qquad (2,3),\qquad (10,11),\qquad \text{query } (3, ?)
Step 1 – distance on the observed feature only. Compare the query with each complete row on $A$ (the only coordinate it has):
Step 2 – pick the $k=2$ nearest. The nearest are row 2 $(d=1)$ and row 1 $(d=2)$.
Step 3 – average their $B$ values.
The completed row is $(3,\,2.5)$. Row $(10,11)$ was ignored because it is far away, which is exactly the point of a neighbourhood-based fill.

Practical note. sklearn.impute.KNNImputer uses a nan-Euclidean distance, which computes the distance over the coordinates present in both rows and rescales by the number of such coordinates. Features must be scaled first, otherwise the largest-range feature dominates the neighbour search.
Summary
Everything on one page

The KNN Imputer is multivariate: other rows are also

It works on the KNN algorithm — find rows with characteristics
 similar to the incomplete row, and replace the value with the
 nearest neighbours' values.

 $d=\sqrt{\frac{p}{|P|}\sum_{j\in P}(x_j-y_j)^2}$ over the columns present

$k$ is a hyperparameter: small $k$ is noisy, large $k$ converges to the

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. How does the KNN Imputer differ from median imputation?

Median imputation is univariate — it uses only the column being filled, so
every missing value gets the same number. KNN imputation is multivariate: it
finds the $k$ most similar rows using the other columns and averages their
values, so the imputed value is conditioned on the rest of the row. It preserves
correlations that median imputation destroys.

Q. How do you compute the distance when the neighbour rows also have
missing values?

With nan_euclidean: sum the squared differences over the columns present
in both rows, then multiply by $p/|P|$ to rescale as if all columns had been
present. Without that rescaling, rows sharing fewer columns would appear closer.
Q. Why must you scale before KNN imputation?

Because it is distance-based. An unscaled salary column with variance $10^8$
dominates an age column with variance $10^2$, so the "nearest" rows are chosen
almost entirely on salary, and every other column contributes nothing.
Q. What happens as $k$ grows?

The imputed value converges to the column mean — averaging over more and more
neighbours washes out the local information. You have paid $O(n^2p)$ for mean
imputation. Tune $k$ by cross-validation.
Q. When would you not use it?

On large datasets (past roughly $10^5$ rows the quadratic cost is prohibitive),
in high dimensions (distances become uninformative — Topic 32), when the
columns are close to independent (no benefit over the median), and when you
cannot afford to ship the training matrix as part of the model artefact.
Q. Does the KNN Imputer leak?

Not if it is inside a pipeline. It is a fitted transformer: it learns the
training matrix in fit and uses only that matrix to find donors in
transform. Fitting it on the combined train and test data would leak, as
with any transformer.
